reaction_center: The carbonyl-adjacent trifluoroethyl fragment of the electrophile, especially the CF₃-derived carbon that becomes the fluorinated alkene carbon.
The carbon attached to boron in the organoboron coupling partner, which is transferred to form the new C–C bond.
The adjacent carbonyl group, proposed tentatively to direct or assist Pd activation.
The two C–F bonds lost during net conversion of a CF₃-derived center into a product retaining one fluorine.
electrophile_state: Trifluoroethyl carbonyl compound, represented in the mechanism as compound 1.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: a carbonyl-coordinated, chelated five-membered palladium intermediate A.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: a gem-difluoroenone intermediate B formed by β-F elimination; attempted detection or trapping was inconclusive.
The exact palladium-bound electrophile geometry, oxidation state, and stereochemical course are unknown.
nucleophile_state: Organoboron reagent 2 is the carbon-transfer coupling partner.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: the organoboron reagent undergoes transmetalation with Pd-containing intermediate E to form intermediate F.
The operative boron species, its aggregation or hydrolysis state, and whether KHCO₃ directly activates it are unknown.
No nucleophile family beyond organoboron reagents is inferred.
bond_changes: Net formation of a C–C bond between the CF₃-derived alkene carbon of the trifluoroethyl carbonyl substrate and the carbon transferred from the organoboron reagent.
Net conversion of the carbonyl-adjacent trifluoroethyl unit into a monofluoroalkene, requiring net cleavage/loss of two C–F bonds because the product retains one fluorine.
Formation of a C=C bond conjugated with the carbonyl group.
Tentative proposed sequence: a first β-F elimination gives a gem-difluoroenone, and a later β-F elimination after organoboron incorporation gives the monofluoroalkene.
Competing over-defluorination would remove the remaining alkene fluorine to furnish a fully defluorinated alkene.
reactive_intermediates: Tentative chelated five-membered palladium intermediate A.
Tentative gem-difluoroenone intermediate B; trapping or detection was inconclusive.
No radical intermediate has been established.
elementary_steps: Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: carbonyl coordination to Pd and polarization of adjacent C–F bonds.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: formation of chelated five-membered palladium intermediate A.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: base-associated β-F elimination from A to gem-difluoroenone B and Pd-H C.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: conversion of B into migratory-insertion intermediate E.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: transmetalation of E with organoboron reagent 2 to intermediate F.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: β-F elimination from F forms the C–C-coupled monofluoroalkene 3 and regenerates active Pd.
Tentative competing AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: insertion of product 3 with Pd-H C gives Pd(II) intermediate D, followed by β-F elimination to fully defluorinated alkene 4.
No elementary radical step is established by the inhibition experiments.
electronic_requirements: The authors infer that productive reactivity depends on the combined electronic features of both coupling partners; this is an empirical scope interpretation, not a quantified mechanistic requirement.
Highly electron-deficient heteroaryl boron reagents are reported to have limited compatibility.
Strongly coordinating substrates are reported to have limited compatibility.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: carbonyl coordination to Pd polarizes the adjacent C–F bonds.
No redox-potential, acidity, orbital, or quantitative electronic threshold is established.
steric_requirements: The authors infer a combined steric dependence involving both coupling partners.
Sterically congested and ortho-disubstituted arylboron partners are reported to show diminished or limited reactivity.
No quantitative steric threshold or required coordination geometry is established.
catalyst_roles: Pd catalyst is required in the reported controls. SI associates Pd168 with CAS 205319-06-8. Active species and ligand retention remain UNKNOWN; external name resolution is separately audited, not a first-party mechanistic observation.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: Pd coordinates to the substrate carbonyl and polarizes adjacent C–F bonds.
Tentative AUTHOR HYPOTHESIS: Pd supports β-F elimination, migratory insertion, organoboron transmetalation, product-forming β-F elimination, and regeneration of an active palladium species.

The standard HTE setup reports 80 °C for 12 h in a 250 μL total reaction volume.
Reactions were set up under N₂ in a glovebox according to the SI general information.

failed_scope: Reported limited compatibility with highly electron-deficient heteroaryl boron reagents.

A radical pathway remains unresolved: TEMPO inhibition occurred, but differential inhibition by BHT and 1,1-diphenylethylene means the trapping experiments do not establish a radical mechanism.

The manuscript statement that alkyl organoboron reagents were unreactive conflicts with its productive N-Boc-protected piperidinyl boronic-ester model reaction; the classification or boundary intended by 'alkyl organoboron' is unresolved.

principles.experimental_consequence: Matched Seed-condition comparisons that vary one partner feature at a time should determine whether the reported limitations track electronics, coordination, steric congestion, reactive-form stability, or interactions among those variables; no aryl-versus-alkyl boundary is established in advance.
principles.falsifying_experiment: Under otherwise matched Seed conditions, test organoboron partners that independently vary steric congestion, coordination ability, and electronics, including matched cyclic carbon donors with and without the reported protecting-group environment. Quantify reagent persistence, desired coupling, protodeboronation, and over-defluorination. Reproducible performance independent of all varied features would falsify the proposed multivariable dependence, while a resolved and exception-free alkyl boundary would falsify the claim that the family boundary remains unresolved.
known_exceptions: The productive protected piperidinyl boronic-ester model conflicts with the manuscript's alkyl-organoboron failure statement.
Selected heteroaryl or electronically varied partners working in other catalytic systems do not establish Seed compatibility.
A low yield under one ligand or condition does not establish intrinsic partner incompatibility.
mechanistic_basis: The Seed reports combined electronic and steric dependence but supplies no quantitative thresholds.
The operative organoboron species and whether KHCO3 activates it are unknown.
Conditional transferred assessments support organoboron carbon-transfer competence while preserving catalyst, electrophile, and condition mismatches.
Transferred negative scope observations are condition-specific and do not establish family-wide exclusion.

Sterically inhibited coupling.

Highly electron-deficient heteroaryl substitution under the Seed conditions.
Structures or conditions that accelerate organoboron decomposition.

principles.claim: If the proposed carbonyl-bound Pd intermediate, gem-difluoroenone, Pd-H species, or sequential insertion/transmetalation/beta-fluoride-elimination sequence lies on the productive Seed pathway, the relevant intermediate must be structurally supported and kinetically competent under conditions demonstrably connected to the grounded reaction. The supplied net chemistry and inconclusive trapping do not currently establish any complete catalytic sequence.
condition_window: Mechanistic tests should reproduce Pd168, KHCO3, DCE, 80 °C, and N2 where feasible.

principles.experimental_consequence: An independently prepared or generated Seed-relevant gem-difluoroenone can support an on-pathway assignment only if it enters product formation under grounded or explicitly bridged conditions at a rate compatible with turnover; tests of Pd nuclearity, carbonyl involvement, labeling, and radical behavior must distinguish the proposed sequence from supplied alternatives.
principles.falsifying_experiment: Independently prepare or generate a faithful gem-difluoroenone, establish its identity and concentration by orthogonal analysis, and compare its product-forming rate with that of the parent Seed substrate under grounded conditions. Failure to form the Seed product at a kinetically competent rate would falsify its assignment as an obligatory productive intermediate; Pd-order, carbonyl-perturbation, isotope-label, and radical-clock results incompatible with the proposed sequence would falsify the corresponding elementary-step assignments.
known_exceptions: Failure to accumulate an intermediate does not exclude fast reversible formation.
Spectral similarity alone does not establish intermediate identity.
TEMPO inhibition alone does not establish a radical step.
A different Pd nuclearity or ligand state may operate without changing the net bond changes.

principles.claim: In the supplied conditional analogies, a suitably configured beta-fluoro carbon-metal or carbanion-like addition intermediate may undergo beta-fluoride elimination to a fluorinated alkene. applicable_electrophile_families: Fluorinated substrates for which sequential partial and further defluorination are observed or directly tested
Fluorinated alkene products shown to remain susceptible to the operative reaction mixture
applicable_nucleophile_families: Carbon donors compatible with the tested catalytic mixture
catalyst_requirements: A catalyst system capable of the desired bond construction and partial defluorination.

principles.claim: Where a partially defluorinated intermediate or product remains reactive in the operative mixture, the desired fluorination state can be a kinetic stopping point rather than an intrinsic endpoint. The Seed and conditional transferred evidence justify testing temperature, base, reagent stoichiometry, fluoride activity, water content, and residence time as system-specific variables, but they do not establish a universal direction or magnitude for those effects.
condition_window: Begin from a productive baseline and vary condition dimensions independently where feasible.
Use ion-pair, salt, and scavenger controls before assigning an effect to fluoride activity.
Control water content and distinguish effects on donor activation, catalyst speciation, hydrolysis, and elimination.
Use time-resolved calibrated product measurements and product-resubjection controls rather than endpoint isolated yield alone.
principles.experimental_consequence: For an applicable system, time or condition changes should alter the distribution between partial defluorination, further defluorination, and decomposition independently of total conversion; the direction must be established experimentally for that system.
principles.falsifying_experiment: Starting from a productive baseline, perform time courses that independently vary temperature, base identity or loading, donor-to-electrophile ratio, controlled water, and selected fluoride scavengers. Include isolated-product resubjection and calibrated crude-versus-isolated analysis. If the verified partially defluorinated species is not consumed and fluorination-state distributions remain invariant across the validated window, the kinetic-stopping-point principle is falsified for that system.
known_exceptions: Some fluorinated products may be persistent across the tested window.
Water or salts may affect organoboron or catalyst speciation without directly controlling fluoride loss.
Stoichiometric effects may reflect conversion or catalyst concentration rather than sequential product reaction.
Transferred systems establish condition sensitivity only in their own bounded settings.
The supplied product-recovery failure is explicitly structure-specific and cannot be generalized to all monofluoroalkenes.
mechanistic_basis: The Seed reports more over-defluorination with stronger base or higher temperature.
Conditional assessments support system-specific control of defluorination count by conditions without transferring their catalytic cycles.
Unknown and non-transferable assessments identify water, salt, stoichiometry, stereochemical evolution, and workup recovery as testable cautions rather than established shared mechanisms.
predicted_failure_modes: Further defluorination during prolonged catalyst exposure.
Hydrolysis, protic addition, or decomposition after initial product formation.
Organoboron decomposition under altered water or salt conditions.
Misleading isolated yields caused by structure-specific workup instability.
Incorrect selectivity estimates from uncalibrated analytical response.
principles.required_reactive_form: A verified partially defluorinated product or intermediate that remains exposed to a reagent or catalyst capable of further C-F loss or pathway diversion.
structural_inhibitors: Products shown to undergo catalyst reinsertion, reduction, hydrolysis, or nucleophilic addition.
Structures whose remaining C-F bond is activated under the productive conditions.
Functional groups shown to impair workup persistence.
structural_promoters: A partially defluorinated product with low affinity for the active catalyst.
Features that slow subsequent activation without blocking initial bond construction.
Conditions that remove or quench the product before further reaction.
principles.title: Partial defluorination as a conditional kinetic stopping point

evidence.claim: The authors propose that hemiacetal salt 30 is in equilibrium with ring-opened lithium alkoxide 31; acid quenching liberates hydroxy compounds 32 and 33, and an unstable protonated hemiacetal is proposed to rearrange to 36, which eliminates HF to give furanone 28.
evidence.quotation:
Hemiacetal salt 30 formed in the reaction of 1 with RLi is very probably in equilibrium with the ring opened lithium alkoxide 31.
From the lithium salts, free hydroxy compounds 32 and 33 are liberated by quench- ing the reaction mixture with triﬂuoroacetic acid.
Protonated hemiacetal 34 is an unstable intermediate that rearranges to 36.
The transfer of water species on the allylic system can be intermolecular (35) or intramolecular ( 37) and leads a-ﬂuoro hydroxy compound 36.
This immediately eliminates hydrogen ﬂuoride to give the end 3(2 H)-furanone 28.
The liberated HF acts as the catalyst and the rearrangement is thus auto- catalysed.

evidence.claim: The authors propose that azide first substitutes the vinyl fluorine to form a vinyl azide, followed either by azirine formation and rearrangement or by direct 5-exo-trig cyclization through enolate oxygen attack; nitrogen release is proposed as the driving force.
evidence.quotation:
Nucleophilic substitution of vinyl F atom by azide anion affords vinyl azide intermediate A (A-1 and A-2 as its resonance structures), upon which two possible path- ways may account for the formation of isoxazole: (1) 3- exo-trig cyclization of A-1 gives the intermediate azirine B, which is con- verted to the product 3a via intramolecular rearrangement (path A).
(2) Alternatively, direct 5- exo-trig cyclization of A-2 via enolate O-attack affords the isoxazole product (path B).
In either reaction pathways, releasing N 2 was the driving force to promote efﬁcient cyclization.

evidence.claim: The authors propose a mechanism involving Cs2CO3-assisted HF elimination, nucleophilic addition/fluoride elimination to form a coupled species, further desaturation and aromatization, and intramolecular O-nucleophilic vinylic substitution that cleaves a fourth C-F bond; they state that a 5-endo-trig pathway cannot be excluded.
evidence.quotation:
On the basis of the abovementioned control experim ents, DFT calculations, and literature survey ( Jaros- chik, 2018 ; Shen et al., 2015 ; Stahl et al., 2013 ), a possible mechanism of the Co(II)-assisted/base-promoted deﬂuorination for the formation of the observed products is described in Scheme 5 .
Initially, a rapid nucle- ophilic 1,4-addition/ﬂuoride elimination event of the N- or S-nucleophile with a,b-unsaturated carbonyl compound A, which is in situ generated from substrate 1 by spontaneously removing a molecule of HF Figure 3.
with the assistance of Cs 2CO3, occurs to give the b-coupled species C.
Subsequently, tautomerization of nascent C affords a more stable endocyclic naphthalen-1(4 H)-one D.N e x t ,b,g-desaturation readily pro- ceeds in the presence of Cs 2CO3 by extrusion of the third ﬂuoride ion to produce the transient intermediate E, mainly owing to the p-conjugated effect.
The subsequent formation of a naphthol/phenol anion F may be explained by a base-assisted elimination of a proton at C4-position of E, and autoaromatization greatly contributes to the driving force of this step ( Pigeon et al., 2010 ).
Finally, occurrence of an intramolecular O- nucleophilic vinylic substitution ( Li et al., 2013 )( SNV; via intermediate F) delivers the ring-closure products 3-18 via readily cleaving the fourth C-F bond.
On the other hand, the possibility that the reaction proceeds through 5- endo-trig cyclization could not be ruled out ( Ichikawa et al., 2002 ).
evidence.section_context: Mechanism Study: Proposed mechanism
evidence.visual_review_reference: Scheme 5 on PDF page 13 contains the proposed structures and requires visual review for structure-level interpretation.

evidence.quotation:
Experimental Section General Procedure for the Allylic Cyanation Under argon atmosphere Rh(PPh3)Cl (6.60 mg, 7.00 μmol) and phosphite 10 (18.4 mg, 28.0 μmol) were dissolved in THF and warmed to 70 °C for 15 min.
The solution was cooled to rt and trifluoroacetate rac-12 a (50.0 mg, 0.14 mmol) and TMSCN (0.09 mL, 0.71 mmol) were added subsequently.
The resulting slightly yellow solution was warmed to 70 °C and stirred for 4 h.
It was quenched with saturated aqueous NaHCO3 solution and the aqueous layer was extracted with diethyl ether (3 × 20 mL).
The combined organic layers were dried over MgSO4 and the solvent was removed under reduced pressure.
The crude product was purified by flash chromatography on silica (n- pentane/diethyl ether 70:1) providing nitrile rac-13 a (26.0 mg, 0.10 mmol, 72%, Z/E= 11:1) as colourless oil.

evidence.claim: Fluorinated substrates gave exclusively the distal regioisomer in the reported scope, whereas the corresponding nonfluorinated substrate produced a 2:1 distal/proximal mixture, supporting a decisive fluorine substituent effect on regioselectivity.
evidence.quotation:
The complete regioselectivity for the distal product in all cases in scheme 2 is remarkable.
Electronic effects can influence the regioselectivity of the allylic substitution.[1] The electron-withdrawing CF3-group favors the distal product while an electron-donating OMe-group leads often to the proximal product.[15] In order to clarify the influence of the fluorine substitu- ent, the corresponding nonfluorinated compound 14 was prepared and subjected to the standard cyanation conditions (Scheme 3).
For this case, a 2:1 mixture of the distal product 15 and the proximal product 16 was formed.
Thus, the presence of the fluorine substituent is crucial for complete regioselectivity observed.

No stereo- erosion was observed for the allylic substitution of trifluoroacetate 12 j into the 3-fluoroallylic nitrile 13 j.
The stereochemical outcome of the allylic cyanation (12 j!13 j) was proven by determination of the absolute configuration of the stereocenter.
Reduction of the nitrile and subsequent Cbz-protection gave alkene 20.
Ozonolytic cleavage of the double bond and subsequent NaBH4 reduction led to alcohol (S)-21, which was independently synthesized from the known corresponding β-amino acid (for details see supporting information).[17] This confirms experimentally that the allylic cyanation occurs with inversion of the stereo- center.

evidence.quotation:
How- ever, while ﬂuoride is the weakest 1e-reducing agent among the halide anions, it is the strongest base and (in aprotic organic solvents) nucleophile.
30 The detailed product and kinetic analysis which was done in their thorough work unequivocally proved that the “RO-adduct anion of p- benzoquinone is a real electron donor and that RO − is acting as a very strong base or nucleophile rather than a one-electron reductant in an aprotic solvent, such as MeCN ”.30 Apparently, the F− anions react with p-benzoquinones in a similar way.
30 An analysis of the HOMO energies supports the suggestion that σ-complexes act as reducing agents.
As such, the appearance of DDQ − (and, to a less extent, other anion radicals) in the presence of ﬂuoride is related to the reduction of DDQ by the σ-complex, DDQ·F−, which is a stronger reducing agent than iodide.
While the detailed mechanistic analysis of the reduction of p- benzoquinones in the presence of F − anions is beyond the scope of the current work, the data obtained herein revealed the distinct nature of their complexes with p-benzoquinones.
The appearance of anion radicals in the solutions containing ﬂuorides is related to the strong nucleophilic character of these anions, leading to the formation and follow-up reactions of the σ-complexes (analogous to that described by Fukuzumi et al.30). ■ CONCLUSIONS The study of the interaction of halides with p-benzoquinone acceptors provided an opportu nity to evaluate spectral, thermodynamic, and structural features of the complexes formed solely via anion −π bonding.

Based on the results of the above-mentioned control experiments, a radical ﬂuoroalkylation/deﬂuorination/annula- tion mechanism consisting of three successive steps is shown in Scheme 8 .
In initial photocatalytic step 1, an excited-state EY* with reducing ability is generated from Na 2-EY by irradiation with visible light (eosin Y, λexc = 539 nm),10 and a single electron transfer (SET) from this species to ﬂuoroalkyl halide occurs to produce an electrophilic n-C4F9 radical and a radical cation EY+.
Next, generation of tertiary carbocation B via the addition of a perﬂuoroalkyl radical to the C C bond of silyl enol ether, followed by further oxidation with the aid of the oxidative radical cation EY+, takes place, owing to the high reduction potential of α-silyloxy intermediate A.11 After rapid attack by an I − ion, the formed unstable intermediate B would decompose to give α- perﬂuoroalkylated ketone C.11 In de ﬂuorination step 2, α,β- desaturation of carbonyl compound C is enabled by eliminating a molecule of HF under basic conditions.
12 Finally, ring closure (step 3) involving intermolecular [3 + 3] condensation of 4a′ with amidine 1 proceeds to furnish the desired pyrimidine 4.

Friedel−Crafts-Type Cyclization of 2,2-Difluorovinyl Ketones via r-Fluorocarbocations and Its Application in Domino Cyclizations Junji Ichikawa,*,† Mikio Kaneko,‡ Misaki Yokota,† Masaaki Itonaga,‡ and Takaharu Yokoyama‡ Department of Chemistry, Graduate School of Science, The Uni Versity of Tokyo, Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo 113-0033, Japan, and Department of Applied Chemistry, Kyushu Institute of Technology, Sensui-cho, Tobata, Kitakyushu 804-8550, Japan junji@chem.s.u-tokyo.ac.jp Received April 14, 2006 ABSTRACT 2,2-Difluorovinyl ketones bearing an aryl group undergo Friedel −Crafts-type cyclization via carbocations stabilized by r-fluorines on treatment with a trimethylsilylating agent [Me 3SiOTf or Me 3SiB(OTf)4].

evidence.quotation:
Based on these experimental results and previously published reports found in the literature, 15 a plausible mechanism for this nucleophilic ﬂuorinated pathway was proposed ( Scheme 5 ).
Reaction of 1a with Select ﬂuor produces intermediate I via an electrostatic interaction between the ammonium site of Select ﬂuor and the ketone.
Then formation of the ﬁnal product 2a may go through two possible pathways, with the tetra ﬂuoroborate anion in syn and anti to the aldehyde group, respectively.
However, the ﬂuoride transfer of tetra ﬂuoroborate anion in path a is more favorable than the ﬂuoride transfer in path b due to the chelation between tetraﬂuoroborate anion and the oxygen present in the aldehyde group.
After ﬂuoride transfer from the BF 4 − ion, the zwitterionic intermediate II forms through Michael addition, followed by an intramolecular cyclization, 16,19 which explains the trans alkene geometry in intermediate II in a simultaneous fashion.
Finally, hydrolysis of intermediate II furnishes the ﬁnal product ( E)-2a.20 In conclusion, we have developed a novel intramolecular carboﬂuorination reaction of α,β-ynones, leading to highly substituted monoﬂuoroalkene via simultaneous construction of C−C and C −F bonds.

evidence.claim: The authors propose dual activation in which tritylium activates the acyl-fluoride carbonyl, BF4 supplies the initial fluoride, and collapse of a tetrahedral intermediate expels fluoride to regenerate TrBF4; cyclization and fluoride addition may be concerted or stepwise.
evidence.quotation:
Instead, we propose that the reaction proceeds through a dual activation pathway where the trityl cation activates the C�O bond of the acyl fluoride (intermediate B′), increasing theelectrophilicity of the carbonylcarbon, while BF4 − serves as the initial fluoride donor.
This is in line with literature reports of trityl cations acting as Lewis acid activators for a range of alcohols and carbonyl moieties.23,24,29 The cyclization and fluoride addition steps may be stepwise or concerted.
Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate B″ forms the carbonyl moiety and expels a fluoride ion to regenerate the TrBF4 catalyst.

evidence.claim: Catalytic activity depended strongly on both Lewis-acid identity and the BF4 counterion: changing BF4 to PF6 or BArF20 nearly stopped catalysis, while BCl3 and BBr3 produced halogen-exchange products.
evidence.quotation:
Though other boron trihalide species were similarly reactive to BF3·OEt2, halogen exchange products were also observed (entries 2 and 3).
Further screening of carbon- based Lewis acids (entries 9 and 10) with a BF4 − counterion revealed that the yields strongly correlate to the Lewis acidity of the carbocation (TrBF4 > MeOTrBF4 > TroBF4).24 Switching the counterion from BF4 − to PF6 − (entry 11) or BArF20 (entry 12) led to almost a complete cessation of catalytic activity.
Together, these results reveal the importance of both the fluoride source and the Lewis acid identity for the fluoroacylation reaction.

evidence.claim: Anhydrous lithium hydroxide converted hexafluorotropone into pentafluorotropolone at room temperature in benzene, affording an approximately 85% pure product in 72% yield based on consumed hexafluorotropone.
evidence.quotation:
In a 50 mL round-bottom flask was dissolved hexafluorotropone (0.28 g, 1.3 mmol) in benzene (20 mL).
Anhydrous lithium hydroxide powder (0.84 g, 35 mmol) was added, and the suspension was stirred at room temperature under nitrogen overnight.
After filtration, the filtrate was evaporated to recover 0.03 g of unreacted tropone 3.
The filter cake was dissolved i n 3 N HCl ( ∼100 mL), and the solution was extracted with ether (100 mL× 3).
The ether solution was washed with water (100 mL) and dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate.
After rotary evaporation, the brown solid residue was sublimed at 60 °C/50 mTorr to give 0.18 g of pentafluorotropolone as a white solid, ∼85% pure, 72% yield based on consumed tropone 3.
evidence.section_context: Experimental preparation of pentafluorotropolone (21) from hexafluorotropone (3).

evidence.claim: The authors proposed that transmetalation could generate a nickel-nucleophile species, followed by CO insertion and formal oxidative addition of the trifluoromethylated alkyl iodide; reductive elimination from the resulting high-valent nickel species was proposed to produce the product while suppressing beta-fluoride elimination.
evidence.quotation:
To realize this nickel-catalyzed process, two crucial issues should be addressed: one is how to suppress the formation of unreactive carbonylnickel complexes under the atmosphere of CO ( Scheme 1B); the other is how to suppress the β-ﬂuoride elimination of tri ﬂuoromethylated secondary alkyl iodides 1 that is generally encountered in transition-metal-catalyzed reactions ( Scheme 1 C).11 To solve these problems, we proposed that one possible pathway is to identify a nickel-involved catalysis pathway that can enable the transmetalation with a nucleophile (Nu) to generate a [Nix(Ln)-Nu] ( A), which in parallel suppresses the formation of unreactive Ni(CO) 4 or NiL(CO)3 complexes (Scheme 1D).
The subsequent insertion of CO into [Ni x(Ln)-Nu] provides acylnickel complex [Ni x(Ln)-CONu] ( B), which undergoes formal oxidative addition with 1 to give a high-valence nickel complex [CF 3CH(alkyl)-Nix+2(Ln)-CONu] ( C).
This highly reactive nickel species is prone to reductive elimination to produce the desired product, 12 thus suppressing the β-ﬂuoride elimination.

evidence.claim: L9 increased product formation and meta selectivity under the reported conditions: no more than 20% olefinated product formed without L9 after 20 h, close to 65% formed with 1.0 equivalent L9, and 0.5 equivalent L9 gave 53% yield with o/m/p = 1/3.3/1.
evidence.quotation:
In the absence of hydrogen-bond donor L9, the ole ﬁnation reaction gave no more than 20% of the ole ﬁnated products 3a after 20 h, while under the same conditions, close to 65% of the products were obtained with 1.0 equiv of L9.
Both the reactivity and meta selectivity (53% yield, o/m/p = 1/3.3/1) declined obviously when reducing the loadings of hydrogen-bond donor L9 to 0.5 equiv.
It was found that with a loading of 0.5 equiv L9,C −H ole ﬁnation products were provided in slightly higher yield (58% yield) when further extending the reaction time to 48 h.
evidence.section_context: Parallel experiments testing the effect and loading of hydrogen-bond donor L9.

evidence.claim: NMR and IR measurements support hydrogen-bond association between urea L9 and acceptors, including TPPO, DMSO, benzophenone, aromatic aldehyde, ester, and amide partners.
evidence.quotation:
As compared with L9 (5.81 ppm, 7.62 ppm) in d- chloroform solution, the chemical shifts of two urea N −H protons move down ﬁeld to 6.62 ppm, 9.18 ppm in L9/TPPO 1:1 complex and 6.70 ppm, 9.45 ppm in d6-DMSO solution, respectively ( Figure 1 ), consistent with the previous Scheme 2.
Carbonyl stretching frequencies for L9 are highly sensitive to hydrogen bonding, varying from 1658 cm−1 in L9 to 1712 cm −1 in both 1:1 complexes of L9 with TPPO and benzophenone ( Figure 2 ).
Similarly, urea carbonyl stretching frequencies in 1:1 cocrystals of L9 and aromatic aldehyde, ester and amide also vary from 1658 cm −1 in L9 to 1712 cm −1 (Figure 3).
All IR and NMR data unambiguously supports the occurrence of hydrogen-bonding interaction between L9 and hydrogen-bond acceptors.
evidence.section_context: Spectroscopic and cocrystal evidence for hydrogen-bond formation.

evidence.claim: The authors propose a Ni(I)-involving cycle in which photoexcited TBADT generates an acyl radical from the aldehyde, Ni(I) captures that radical, an alkyl radical oxidizes the resulting acyl–nickel intermediate to Ni(III), and reductive elimination forms the C–C bond.
evidence.quotation:
Meanwhile, although the [W]-2H species (III in Scheme 6) was proposed to have the ability to reduce Ni(I) to Ni(0) in some previous works,14 the recent DFT calculation showcased this process seems very unfavorable.15 Therefore, combined with the above experiment, a Ni(I)-involved mechanism was considered more reasonable, and a proposed catalytic cycle was listed in Scheme 6.
Photoexcitation of TBADT produces the excited state, which can abstract a hydrogen atom from aldehyde to form the sp2-hybridized radical.
This radical would be captured by the Ni(I) species IV to generate the acyl-nickel intermediate V, followed by further oxidization with the alkyl radical to afford the trivalent nickel species VI primed for the carbon−carbon formation.
After the reductive elimination to give the product, the newly formed Ni(I) species would reduce alkyl bromide to produce the alkyl radical with the generation of Ni(II) species VII.
A single-electron transfer between this nickel intermediate and strong reductant III regenerates the nickel catalyst IV thus closing the cycle.

evidence.quotation:
A 100 mL round-bottom ﬂask with magnetic stir bar was ﬁlled with 1.40 g (5.65 mmol) of the crude diaziridine, 60 mL of methylene chloride, and 3.5 mL of triethylamine.
The stirred solution was cooled in an ice bath.

The mixture was stirred in the ice bath until the solid iodine dissolved; then, it was allowed to warm to room temperature and to stir for 1 h.
A solution of 1 N potassium hydroxide (30 mL) was added, and the mixture was vigorously stirred for 30 min.
Water (100 mL) was added, and the mixture was extracted with methylene chloride (3 × 30 mL).
The combined organic extracts were washed with 100 mL of 1 M aqueous HCl solution and 100 mL of water and then dried.
The evaporation of the solvent left 1.3 g of brown oil.
The residue was dissolved in hexane and ﬂushed through a short plug of silica gel using additional hexane as eluent.
The evaporation left a clear colorless oil that was dynamically transferred under high vacuum to a liquid nitrogen cooled U-trap to give 1.0 g (72%) of a very pale pink liquid.
The product was greater than 98% pure when analyzed by capillary GC (30 m dimethylsilicone column, 150 °C injector, 100 °C column temp).

evidence.claim: The proposed mechanism comprises DABCO-mediated peroxide rearrangement and HF elimination to β-fluoro enone B, SNV-type C-F cleavage by the carbanion of 2a to intermediate D, and intramolecular cyclocondensation to product 3.
evidence.quotation:
On the basis of the results presented above and literature reports, a plausible mechanism for this [3 + 3] annulation reaction was proposed ( Scheme 3 ).
The DABCO-mediated Kornblum−De La Mare rearrangement of peroxide 1a and the further elimination of one molecule of HF a ﬀords the key β- ﬂuoro enone B.
Then S NV-type C−F bond cleavage of B with the carbanion of 2a preferentially and readily produces the intermediate D.
Subsequent intramolecular cyclocondensation via E leads to the formation of the desired per ﬂuoroalkylated product 3.

According to current findings and preceding research , we proposed a preliminary mechanism for this c arbofluorination reaction (Scheme 4c).
Firstly, the oxidative addition of gem-DFCP 1a with [Rh(CO)2(BINAP)BF4] catalyst gives the intermediate A, which then undergoes β-F elimination to deliver the fluoroallyl Rh species B.
Subsequently, the outer-sphere nucleophilic attack of styrene 2a on intermediate B can generate a benzylic cation C.
This carbocation C finally leads to the production of fluoride 3a by abstracting a fluoride from a BF4-, along with the formation of one molecular BF3.21 The resulting BF3 can react with fluoride ions to form BF4- and regenerate the rhodium catalyst.
This is our preliminary understanding of the reaction mechanism, and the detailed process will be further elucidated by combining it with DFT (density functional theory) calculations in the near future.

evidence.claim: The reported transformation is a defluorinative carboimination in which a trifluoromethyl-ketone-derived substrate undergoes C-F cleavage and formation of C-C and C=N bonds to furnish alpha,alpha-difluoroimines.
evidence.quotation:
Herein, we report an unprecedented deﬂuorinative carboimination of triﬂuoromethyl ketones via a strategy of silver carbene-initiated rearrangement, in which both C–F bond and carbonyl group of the triﬂuoromethyl ketones were functionalized simultaneously, thus providing a straightforward synthetic method for medicinally relevant α,α-diﬂuoroimines.

evidence.claim: For heteroarenes with multiple nonequivalent nitrogen atoms, fluorovinylation generally occurs at the least sterically hindered nitrogen. An amino-substituted indazole reacts at the indazole nitrogen while retaining its amino group, whereas hydroxy- and hydroxymethyl-substituted indazoles can undergo both O- and N-fluorovinylation.

In general, we observe selective fluorovinylation at the least sterically hindered nitrogen for (NH)-heteroarenes with multiple, nonequivalent nitrogen centers (1a–1c, 1f–1g, 1j, 1m, 1o, 1q–1s, 1v, 1w).
Notably, 7-amino-1H-indazole (1q) selectively undergoes fluorovinylation at N-2 of the indazole, leaving the amino group intact.
In contrast, 7-hydroxy-1H-indazole (1r) undergoes fluorovinylation at both the phenolic hydroxyl group and N-2.

evidence.claim: The authors propose sequential Lewis-acid-mediated defluorination, SMe2 attack, and demethylation events, including an SN1-type initial activation and possible alternative routes to a fluorothioacetal intermediate, followed by a third defluorination and final demethylation.
evidence.quotation:
The mechanism of the defluorination/thioester synthesis is thought to proceed via an initial defluorination of the trifluor- omethyl group by BF 3, followed by attack from SMe 2, resulting in intermediate I (Scheme 1).
The higher reactivity of electron- rich substrates suggest that this occurs via an S N1-type mecha- nism in accordance with other Lewis acid mediated defluorina- tion processes.15 Following this, demethylation of the thionium ion occurs to give II, followed by abstraction of a second fluorine, resulting in intermediate III.
Intermediate III should be highly electrophilic, and react readily with a second SMe 2 molecule, which after demethylation results in the fluoro- thioacetal intermediate IV.
Alternatively, intermediate IV can also be formed by an S N2-type attack by SMe2 on intermediate II followed by demethylation (Scheme 1, dotted line).
Intermedi- ate IV is then converted into V via a third defluorination and this is followed by a final demethylation to form the methyl- dithioester product, compound 1b.

evidence.claim: Chapter 1 independently demonstrates copper(I)-catalyzed selective removal of one fluorine from gem-difluoroalkenes to form stereodefined terminal monofluoroalkenes; diboron and hydrosilane systems provide opposite alkene stereoselectivity.
evidence.quotation:
14 Abstract The author reports a novel approach for the stereodivergent hydrodefluorination of gem-difluoroalkenes using copper(I) catalysts to obtain stereodefined monofluoroalkenes.
Both ( Z)- and ( E)-terminal monofluoroalkenes were obtained by hydrodefluorination of gem-difluoroalkenes in the presence of copper(I) catalysts and diboron or hydrosilane, respectively, with high stereoselectivity.
We found that the copper(I)-catalyzed reaction with diboron proceeded with perfect Z-selectivity (E/Z=1:>99, Scheme 1a).
Furthermore, we found that the stereoselectivity of the defluorination of gem-difluoroalkenes could be drastically switched by swapping the diboron reagent for a hydrosilane (E/Z= from 90:10 to >99:1, Scheme 1b) for the first time.

evidence.claim: The defluorination accommodated aromatic, aliphatic, heterocyclic, sulfur-containing, and amine-containing trifluoromethyl ketones, but quinoline substrate 1Q initially gave only 20% difluorinated product and 35% monofluorinated product.
evidence.quotation:
Functional groups such as chloro (3F), thiomethyl (3G), ben- zyloxy (3H), amine (3I and 3J), and dioxo (3K) groups were well-tolerated, with the reactions proceeding smoothly.
Furthermore, heterocyclic ketones, including pyrrole (1O, 1P), quinoline (1Q), indole (1R), ben- zofuran (1S), and benzothiophene (1T), underwent the trans- formation to produce the corresponding difluoromethyl ke- tones 3O–3T.
However, in the case of quinoline (1Q), the yield of product 3Q was limited to 20%, with the corre- sponding monofluorinated compound 4Q obtained in 35% yield.
Notably, the reaction was not limited to aromatic ketones; aliphatic trifluoromethyl ketone 1U also participated, albeit with lower yields, affording difluoromethyl ketone 3U.

Based on these results, the proposed reaction mechanism is depicted in Figure 4E.
Trifluoromethyl ketones undergo Pu- dovik addition followed by a phospha-Brook rearrangement, leading to β-fluoride elimination and the formation of enol phosphinate and HF.
In the presence of MS4A, HF is effi- ciently trapped, favoring the formation of difluoroenol phos- phinate 2Aa.
In the absence of a trapping agent, protonation occurs, yielding difluoromethyl ketone 3A.

evidence.claim: The authors propose sequential electron transfer and dehalogenation through alkenyl radical A, intermediate 3a, a Lewis-acid-activated carbonyl complex B, alkyl radical C, alpha-CF3 anion D, and final beta-fluoride elimination.
evidence.quotation:
Based on the above mechanistic exploration and related liter - ature reports, [15] we proposed a plausible reaction pathway for this transformation, as outlined in Scheme 6.
Initially, the sub - strate 1a receives an electron from Zn and then undergoes the loss of Cl ‒ to form the alkenyl radical A.
Subsequently, the inter - mediate A could be immediately reduced to 3a by the in-situ-generated Zn+ and render a Zn2+ complex at the same time.
Importantly, this Zn 2+ complex exhibits strong Lewis acid proper - ties and is capabl e of activating the carbonyl group of 3a to form the intermediate B.
After a single -electron reduction-protonation process, the alkyl radical C is generated in the presence of Zn.
Further reduction of radical C produces the α -CF3 anion D, which ultimately undergoes β-F elimination to generate the final product 2a.

A plausible catalytic cycle for the Rh(I) -catalyzed defluorina- tive arylation of pentafluoroethyl alkenes 1 is proposed based on DFT calculations [15] to account for the enantioselectivity and E/Z selectivity (Scheme 8).
First, transmetalation between arylboronic acid and Rh(I)-catalyst in the presence of ( R)-DM-SEGPHOS gener- ates an aryl-rhodium species with chiral ligand.[12,13b] Coordination of the alkene (E)-1a leads to either INT-1A or INT-1B.

Next, β-fluoride elimination at the rhodium centre of INT-2 via transition state TS-2A determines the alkene geometry resulting in product ( Z)-2a.

evidence.claim: The authors propose that DBU-mediated deprotonation forms IN1 and aldehyde addition forms oxygen-anion intermediate IN2; for R = CF3, the proposed pathway proceeds through beta-O elimination and loss of trifluoromethylsulfonate, whereas for R = Me it proceeds through benzoyl 1,3-migration followed by olefination.
evidence.quotation:
DFT calculations for the reaction mechanism As mentioned earlier, to gain further insight into this ﬂuorooleﬁnation reaction, we propose a plausible mech- anism based on experiments and DFT calculations (Scheme 2).
Substrate 1 abstracted hydrogen by the base DBU to obtain intermediate IN1.
Oxygen anion interme- diate IN2 can be produced via nucleophilic addition of IN1 with 2- ﬂuorobenzaldehyde 2m.
When the R group is triﬂuoromethyl, the reaction proceeds through β-O elimi- nation via b-TS2, which is the rate-determining step.
Then triﬂuoromethylsulfonate is removed and produces the vinylcarbonyl product 4a.
When the R group is methyl, the reaction proceeds through benzoyl 1,3-migration via a-TS2 to form a-IN3, where a-TS2 is the rate-determining step.
Compared with tri ﬂuoromethylsulfonate, it is more difﬁcult to release the benzoyloxy unit.
Therefore, a-IN3 subsequently undergoes oleﬁnation via a-TS3 with only a 7.6 kcal/mol energy barrier , generating the vinylsulphonyl product 3rm.

evidence.claim: 作者提出一种可能解释：若反应遵循β-氢化物插入/β-氟消除路径，插入可产生20a或20b；20a可经β-氟消除并继续催化循环，而缺少β-氟取代基的20b不能重返循环，因此插入步骤的区域选择性可能决定催化效率。
evidence.quotation:
The poor efficiency may be explained by looking at the proposed reaction mechanism (scheme 3.4): In the activation step, 18 is supposed to react with the silane to form the catalytically active hydride 19.
Assuming a β-hydride insertion/β-fluoride elimination route, two intermediates 20a and 20b are possible.
20a can undergo a β-fluoride elimination to yield the product 4 and titanocene(III) fluoride (21); reconversion to the active hydride 19 by reaction with a silane molecule closes the catalytic cycle.
20b does not have a β-fluorine substituent and cannot reenter the catalytic cycle.

evidence.claim: Tether length strongly affected coupling: N-propylpicolinamide gave no difluorovinyl-coupled product, N-butenyl- and N-pentenylpicolinamides gave 85% and 52%, and N-hexylpicolinamide lacked reactivity.
evidence.quotation:
When N- propylpicolinamide was subjected to the coupling reaction, no difluorovinyl-coupled product was formed.
This can be attributed to the ring strain associated with the formation of bicyclic 5,4-membered nickelacycles during the migratory vinyl insertion.
In contrast, reactions with N-butenylpicolinamide and N-pentenylpicolinamide yielded the corresponding coupled products in 85% and 52% yields, respectively.
These transformations likely proceed through 5,5- and 5,6-membered bicyclic nickelacycle intermediates, which are relatively favorable.
The lack of reactivity observed with N-hexylpicoli- namide is consistent with the hypothesis that the formation of a 5,7-membered nickelacycle is disfavored under the current conditions.16 To assess whether any radical intermediates are involved in the cross-coupling reactions, we conducted the catalytic reaction in the presence of BHT and (1-cyclopropylvinyl)- benzene (3.0 equiv) as radical scavengers.
evidence.section_context: Mechanistic Study; chain-length scope and proposed nickelacycle-size rationale. Only the observed yields and failures are treated as experimental facts here.

evidence.claim: The authors propose sulfonyl-radical generation by photoexcited Ru(II), radical addition, capture by Ni(II) to form an alkyl-Ni(III) species, beta-fluoride elimination to product, and single-electron transfer that regenerates the catalysts.
evidence.quotation:
Based on previous reports, 4h,7 a plausible mechanism of this radical defluorinative sulfonylation is shown in Scheme 4.
Firstly, sodium benzenesulfonate is preferentially oxidized by photo-excited RuII(bpy)3 to generate the corresponding sulfonyl radical and RuI complex.
Then, radical addition occurs between the sulfonyl radical and 2a to form a benzyl carbon radical I, which can further react with Ni II to form alkyl-Ni III species II.
Next, the final product 3a is obtained via a b-F elimination from II, and at the same time Ni III-F is generated.
Finally, Ru II(bpy)3 and Ni II are regenerated via a single electron transfer between the RuI complex and Ni III-F and the catalytic cycle is completed (Scheme 5).

evidence.claim: The authors propose a simplified mechanism involving C-C activation by oxidative addition, C-F activation by beta-fluoride elimination, and C-C formation by allylic coupling; they speculate that allylic coupling is net stereoretentive and suggest either an inner-sphere metalation/reductive-elimination sequence or allyl-Rh stereoinversion followed by outer-sphere substitution.
evidence.quotation:
Based on these observations and the previous investigations on allylation chemistry, [20] we presented a simplified mechanism for the asymmetric allylation reaction, which includes three processes: C−C activation via oxidati ve addition, C−F activation via β -F elimination and C−C formation via allylic coupling (Scheme 4d).
As the oxidative addition and β-F elimination should be stereoretentive, and net stereoretention was observed for the reaction, we speculate that the third step (allylic coupling) should also be also in net stereoretention.
The net stereoretentive allylation process can occur via an inner-sphere electrophilic C−H metalation/reductive elimination sequence that is similar with our previous study,[10a] or via a stereoinversion of the allyl Rh species followed by an outer-sphere allylic substitution.

evidence.claim: The proposed ketone-coupling pathway involves Pd(0)-mediated cyclopropane C-C and C-F cleavage to an allyl-Pd(II) complex, reaction with a base-generated enol to form a bis(eta1-allyl) intermediate, and reductive elimination; subsequent base-mediated steps produce the furan.
evidence.quotation:
The catalytic cycle was initiated by the oxidative addition of gem- DFCPs to Pd(0), accompanied by C –C bond activation and C –F bond cleavage, to generate the crucial allyl-Pd (II) complex 91.
This intermediate then underwent a transmetalation reac - tion with enol 97, which was generated in situ through base- mediated deprotonation of ketone 89, forming the key bis (η1-allyl) intermediate 93 along with its isomerization prod- uct 94.

The ﬁnal furan product 90 was formed through a base- mediated sequence involving enolization, nucleophilic sub- stitution, and rearomatization, which was promoted by the less sterically hindered Pd catalyst system.

evidence.claim: Two alternative pathways were proposed for conversion of the alpha-aminoalkyl radical into the quinolizidine product, and both include an additional fluoride-elimination event or formation of a fluoroalkenyl biradical followed by intramolecular coupling.
evidence.quotation:
Two possible paths were proposed by the authors for the formation of quinolizidine 102a from radical F.
In path (a), radical addition to C=C double bond generated radical G, followed by single-electron reduction with Ir(II) led to carbanion H and β-fluoride eliminat ion giving final product 102a.
Alternatively, in the path (b) C=C double bond could be reduced by Ir(II) followed by the elimination of fluoride to form fluoroalkenyl biradical I.
The formation of quinolizidine 102a occurred via intramolecular coupling of biradical intermediate I.

evidence.claim: The review defines transfer fluorination as defluorination of a fluorocarbon to generate nucleophilic fluoride, followed by fluorination of an electrophile; the process breaks and creates C-F bonds and is typically stepwise and stoichiometric.
evidence.quotation:
Recycling fluoride (F–) from fluorocarbons Transfer fluorination Transfer fluorination can be defined as a reaction sequence that involves first defluorination of a fluorocarbon to generate a nucleo- philic source of fluoride (F–), which is subsequently used for the fluori- nation of an electrophile.
This reaction involves both breaking and creation of a carbon–fluorine bond.
Typically, a donor molecule con- taining one or more fluorine atoms is defluorinated to form fluoride, which is then used directly in the fluorination of an acceptor molecule.
Transfer fluorination is a stepwise process that relies on use of stoi- chiometric reagents.
evidence.section_context: Recycling fluoride (F-) from fluorocarbons: Transfer fluorination

Moreover, in cases that defluorination can be achieved, there is the potential to generate highly unstable intermedi- ates (e.g. primary alkyl radicals or cations) that may exhibit undesired side reactions rather than engaging in fluoride shuttling.

The resulting solution was stirred at –78 °C for 30 min, and then at rt for 2 h.

One-Pot Sequence Converting Ketones to Fluoroalkenes 2.8a–c An oven-dried round flask (25 mL) was charged with ketone 2.7a–c (0.50 mmol), TPSH (0.50 mmol) and a magnetic stir bar.
A pre-prepared stock solution of TF A (0.050 mmol) in THF (1.0 mL) was added and the reaction mixture was stirred at rt for 1.5 h.
Then, the reaction solution was diluted with additional THF (1.5 mL) followed by the addition of activated 4Å mol ecular sieves (400 mg) and stirred at rt for 10 min.
The solution was cooled to –78 °C, and then n-BuLi (1.5 mmol) was added dropwise into the pre-cooled and stirred solution at –78 °C.
The resulting solution w as stirred at –78 °C for 30 min to generate the dianion and at 0 °C for 20 min to release N 2.
Subsequently, the reaction solution was cooled to –78 °C, and then a solution of NFSI (0.75 mmol, c = 0.50 M in THF) was added dropwise over 4 min.
The resulting solution was stirred at – 78 °C for 30 min, and then at rt for 2 h.

evidence.claim: The proposed catalytic cycle involves formation of a phosphine-coordinated Cu(I)-boryl complex, difluoroalkene insertion into the Cu–B bond to give a beta-borylalkyl copper species, conformational selection, beta-fluoride elimination to form the (Z)-fluorinated alkenylboronate, and regeneration of the Cu-boryl catalyst.
evidence.quotation:
Based on the above observations and previous reports, 24 the mechanism for the Cu-Catalyzed stereoselective borylation of gem-diﬂuoroalkenes with B 2pin2 is proposed ( Scheme 5 ).
Initially, transmetalation of the phosphine-ligated copper catalyst LCuOtBu, which is generated in situ from LCu(OAc) and NaOtBu, with the diboron reagent B 2pin2 provides nucleophilic phosphine-coordinated Cu(I)-boryl complexes LCu −Bpin.
Subsequently, insertion of a di ﬂuoroalkene into the Cu −B bond of borylcopper complex would lead to the generation of β- borylalkyl copper species I.
Rotation of the key intermediate I by ±60° results in the formation of two conformations, II and III.
The intermediate III was relatively unstable due to steric repulsion between the bulky boryl group and the aryl group.
β- Fluoride elimination of borylalkyl copper intermediate II aﬀords the desired pure ( Z)-ﬂuorinated pinacol alkenylboronate along with LCuF.
Finally, LCuF further reacts with B2pin2 and NaOtBu to regenerate the active catalyst LCu −Bpin and ﬁnish the catalytic cycle.

It can be concluded that the barbiturate and trans-β- nitrostyrene substrates for the MA reaction catalyzed by the ZnY bimetallic catalyst are cooperatively activated through their interaction with the Zn and Y metal centers of the catalyst following the proposed mechanism shown in Scheme 1.
In the proposed mechanism, initially the barbiturate substrate is coordinated to the Zn metal center of the 7ZnY catalyst after dissociation of the coordinated DMF solvent molecule and then coordination of the trans-β-nitrostyrene substrate to the Y metal center of the catalyst.
This could be a stepwise process, or both substrates could be simultaneously coordinated to the metal centers of the catalyst yielding the intermediate Im.
The two substrates upon coordination to the metal centers are brought into proximity such that a proton can be transferred from the α-carbon atom of the barbiturate to the CH(NO2) carbon atom of the coordinated trans-β-nitrostyrene followed by the nucleophilic attack of the resulting barbiturate carbanion to the electrophilic C(7) carbon atom of the trans-β- nitrostyrene to yield the intermediate 1Im.
evidence.section_context: Computational studies: proposed cooperative catalytic mechanism

evidence.claim: Unlike the proton, tin, and chlorophosphine electrophiles, MeI did not furnish an isolated metal-functionalized product; it gave P-alkylated phosphine complex 7 and iron complex 6, with unidentified iron-containing by-products inferred from the product distribution.
evidence.quotation:
In contrast to the cases described so far, the reaction of Na[2] with MeI (Scheme 3) a ﬀords no metal-functionalized product but a mixture of a P-alkylated phosphine complex 7 and its iron complex 6 which was isolated in modest yield and characterised by a single-crystal XRD study.
The identity of both species was further established in situ from multinuclear NMR studies and verified by their independent synthesis (see Experimental).
The observed product distribution implies that elemental iron or some iron-containing compounds are formed as by-products, even if none of these was directly identified.

evidence.claim: The authors propose that 8 is a phosphine-bound iron tricarbonyl complex with an empty or solvent-occupied coordination site and may be the initial product of MeI attack; they attribute its conversion to 6 and 7 to ligand extrusion or redistribution.
evidence.quotation:
On this basis, we formulate the product as a complex in which the iron atom is bound to three carbonyls and the neutral phosphine 7, and the remaining coordination site remains empty or is occupied by a solvent molecule ( 8, Scheme 3).
Starting from this assignment, the conversion of 8 into a mixture of 6 and 7 is explained as the consequence of ligand extrusion/redistribution reactions which are common for carbonyl complexes that are coordinatively unsaturated or carry weakly bound solvent ligands.
Considering that the VT NMR studies provided no evidence for the formation of a metal functionalized species as a precur- sor to 8, we consider it likely that this species may indeed con- stitute the initial reaction product.
evidence.section_context: Results and discussion: proposed constitution and mechanistic role of intermediate 8.

evidence.claim: Low-temperature NMR of Na[2] with MeI showed species 8 as approximately 90% of the phosphorus-containing material at −70 °C; it remained unchanged below −50 °C and then irreversibly converted to 6 and 7 on warming to ambient temperature, with no other spectroscopically observed intermediates.
evidence.quotation:
The 1H and 31P NMR spectra recorded immediately after mixing both reactants at −70 °C disclosed that under these conditions a previously unobserved species 8 (Scheme 3) had formed as a major product (approx.
90% of all phosphorus-containing species by integration of the 31P NMR spectrum) besides minor amounts of 6 and 7 (<10%) and trace quantities of unidentified by-products.
The com- position of the reaction mixture did not change perceptibly as long as the temperature was kept below −50 °C.
At this point, the onset of a slow and irreversible conversion of 8 into a mixture of 6 and 7 was noted.
This process accelerated upon warming, and went eventually to completion after the sample had reached ambient temperature.
Further spectroscopically observable intermediates were not detected.

evidence.claim: Temperature can reverse the relative reactivity order of similarly reactive nucleophiles when their activation parameters differ; the paper gives allyltrimethylsilane and 2-methyl-2-butene as an example.
evidence.quotation:
The relative reactivity of the two nucleophiles considered in Figure 10 depends not only on the electrophile but also on the temperature.
At low temperatures, 2-methyl-2- butene is always the stronger nucleophile, but above the aselec- tive temperature, which depends on the electrophile, allyltrime- thylsilane is more reactive than 2-methyl-2-butene.
The effect of temperature is certainly relatively small in gener- al, with the result that large changes in the electrophilicity and nucleophilicity order do not occur with variations in tempera- ture.
If nucleophiles of very similar reactivity but different acti- vation enthalpy (and entropy) are compared, however, a trans- position on the reactivity scale may result.
evidence.section_context: Section 3.5, temperature-dependent nucleophile rankings.

evidence.claim: The authors propose that ketone reduction occurs in the outer coordination sphere without a ketone–ruthenium complex or productive ruthenium alkoxide intermediate, and attribute the high rate and carbonyl selectivity to this nonclassical pathway.
evidence.quotation:
Most notably, unlike in conventional metal hydride reactions (see Scheme 57), the carbonyl oxygen does not interact with the metal center.
Neither a ketone/ruthenium complex nor a ruthenium alkoxide are involved in this reaction mechanism.
The alcohol forms directly from the ketone.
Alcohols may add across the polar Ru ÿN bond of 8 but in a reversible manner, where the resulting ruthenium alkoxides act merely as reservoirs for 8.
Therefore, the ketone reduction does not require any coordinative unsaturation at the ruthenium center but rather occurs in an outer coordina- tion sphere of the 18-electron complex 7 (see Scheme 8b).
This is the main origin of the high rate of this catalytic hydrogenation.
Furthermore, this nonclassical mechanistic model also explains the uncommon functional selectivity in favor of the CO group.
evidence.section_context: Mechanistic interpretation of rate and chemoselectivity.

evidence.claim: The author proposes that excess Lewis acid can lower substrate basicity through adduct formation, forcing protonation to compete with Lewis-acid binding and potentially increasing the required Brønsted acidity by several orders of magnitude.
evidence.quotation:
However, the presence of the Lewis acid, often in large excess, may actually make it more difficult to protonate a substrate.
If the Lewis acid forms an adduct with the substrate, the basicity of the substrate will be significantly lowered.
Protonation of the substrate must then compete with Lewis adduct formation and several orders of magnitude more Brønsted acidity may be required.
We call this phenomenon ‘‘basicity suppression’’ of the substrate and we suspect it is operative in the protonation of benzene and alkenes discussed above.

Reed Received (in Cambridge, UK) 5th October 2004, Accepted 8th February 2005 First published as an Advance Article on the web 25th February 2005 DOI: 10.1039/b415425h Icosahedral carborane anions such as CHB 11Cl11 2 are amongst the least coordinating, most chemically inert anions known.

evidence.claim: Carborane acids readily protonate benzene, and the resulting benzenium carborane salt is reported to remain stable to 150 °C.
evidence.quotation:
Protonated arenes A demonstration of the strength of carborane acids is their ready protonation of benzene.
Triflic acid does not protonate benzene26 and the strongest known neat liquid acid, HFSO 3, (Hammett acidity function H0 52 15.1) does so only to a very small extent.27 Previously, mixed Brønsted/Lewis acids such as HF/SbF5 were necessary to attain acidity high enough to protonate benzene, but this comes at a price.
The presence of SbF5 (in excess, or latently in SbF 6 2 or Sb2F11 2 anions) limits the stability of the resulting benzenium ion to temperatures well below ambient.
On the other hand, when a carborane acid is used, the resulting benzenium ion salt, [C 6H7 +][carborane2], is stable to 150 uC!

evidence.claim: A carborane acid cleanly and reversibly protonates C60 in dry halocarbon solvents, allowing quantitative isolation of the protonated fullerene salt, whereas traditional acids caused oxidative or nucleophilic decomposition.
evidence.quotation:
Protonated C60 A more powerful illustration of the strong-yet-gentle char- acteristics of carborane acids is their protonation of full- erenes.7 A decade of attempts to observe protonation of C 60 with traditional strong and superacids had failed, even working at dry ice temperatures.
This turned out not to be a problem of insufficient acid strength, but rather, a problem of oxidative/nucleophilic decomposition of the fullerene by the conjugate bases of the acids used.
Even the usually non- oxidizing triflic acid was found to decompose C 60, possibly because of the presence of reducible impurities in the acid.
On the other hand, carborane acids such as H(CB 11H5Cl6) cleanly and reversibly protonate C 60 in dry halocarbon solvents.7 The resulting [HC 60 +][carborane2] salt can be isolated in quantitative yield and characterized by novel solid state 13C CPMAS methods32,33 to have a 1,2-carbocation static structure, 3.
evidence.section_context: Protonation of C60 and comparison with decomposition under traditional strong acids.

evidence.quotation:
In principle these methods offer a promising route to a variety of amines, enamines and imines.[125] Unfortunately the direct nucleophilic addition of amines across C-C multiple bonds is hampered by several thermody- namic and kinetic barriers:[125g,126] * Attackoftheaminenitrogenatomthatbearsthelonepair on electron-rich non-activated multiple bonds leads to electrostatic repulsion. * A[ 2+2]-cycloaddition of the N/C0H bond to the alkene is forbidden by thehigh energy difference betweenp(C=C) and s (N/C0H) orbitals. * Because of the highly negative reaction entropy, the reaction is not favored at high temperatures. * The hydroamination reaction is only slightly exothermic or even thermoneutral.[125h] However, the direct nucleophilic addition of amines proceeds easily with
electron-deficient (activated)p-systems containing neighboring functional groups, such as keto, ester, nitrile, sulfoxide, and nitro, which leads to the formation of the anti-Markovnikov products,[127] though the presence of an additional catalyst is found to be advantageous in some cases.

evidence.claim: The computational workflow optimized quinclorac in gas and aqueous phases, evaluated ionic-state energies and atomic charges, and used Gaussian 09.
evidence.quotation:
The optimal conformation was subjected to full geometry reoptimization in the gas phase employing the hybrid B3LYP functional [54-56] and the 6-311++G(2d,2p) basis set [57 ,58].
The optimized herbicide molecules in the gas phase were further reoptimized at the B3LYP/6- 311++G(2d,2p) level employing the PCM solvation model [59,60].
Finally, the optimized B3LYP/6- 311++G(2d,2p) geometries were reoptimized employing the second order Moller Plesset theory (MP2) [61] with the 6-311++G(2d,2p) basis set.
The energy values and atomic charges of the ionic states of quinclorac, cation and anion, were calculated at the B3LYP/6-311++G(2d,2p) and MP2/6- 311++G(2d,2p) levels, in gas and aqueous phases, by using the geometry of the neutral system.
All the calculations reported here were performed with the Gaussian 09 package [62] and visualized with the GaussView V .

evidence.claim: The authors define click chemistry as modular, broad-scope chemistry giving very high yields, inoffensive and readily removable byproducts, and stereospecific outcomes under simple conditions and with simple isolation.
evidence.quotation:
The reaction must be modular, wide in scope , give very high yields , generate only inoffensive byproducts that can be removed by nonchromatographic methods, and be stereospecific (but not necessarily enantio- selective).
The required process characteristics include simple reaction conditions (ideally, the process should be insensitive to oxygen and water), readily available starting materials and reagents, the use of no solvent or a solvent that is benign (such as water) or easily removed , and simple product isolation .
Purification—if required—must be by nonchromatographic methods, such as crystallization or distillation, and the product must be stable under physiological conditions.

evidence.claim: 作者提出如下机理：硼酸与 Al2O3 的 Lewis 碱性位点结合并由表面碱性位点夺取质子；光激发的 Ru(bpy)3(2+) 向吸附的 O2 转移单电子形成超氧物种；随后发生 O-O 键断裂及基团由硼向氧迁移；最后经单电子转移释放酚。
evidence.quotation:
COMMUNICATION From the aforementioned clues elucidating the nature of the selective photocatalytic hydroxylation of boronic acids, the following mechanism is proposed.
The B atom of the boronic acid, being a Lewis acid, binds to the Lewis base site of Al 2O3, while a proton is abstracted from the B(OH) 2 group by the surface base site of Al 2O3 (Scheme 1, step I -II).
Meanwhile, Ru(bpy)32+ is photoexcited to Ru(bpy) 32+*, which donates a single electron to the adsorbed O 2 to form Ru(bpy) 33+ and superoxide (step II-III).
The s uperoxide would accept protons abstracted by the Al2O3 surface base sites and the neighbouring boronic acid groups, resulting in the cleavage of the O -O bond (step III -IV).
The alkyl group would then migrate from the B atom to the O atom that previously co nstituted molecular O 2 (step IV-V).
Single electron transfer from the boronic acid surface complex to Ru(bpy)33+ would then release phenol (step V -I).

evidence.claim: The proposed selectivity model is that bulky alcohols hydrogen-bond to fluoride, replace acetonitrile in its solvation shell, and decrease fluoride basicity so that SN2 is favored over E2.
evidence.quotation:
Consequently, crown ether catalyzed/ mediated fluorination can lead to a substantial side E2 reaction, especially for secondary substrates.43 Aiming to overcome this problem, hydrogen bond donor species such as bulky alcohols can be added to the reaction medium.17 Because these alcohols interact more with the fluoride ion via hydrogen bonding than with the acetonitrile molecules, they can coordinate to the fluoride ion,50 replacing the acetonitrile solvation shell and creating a preferential solvation by the alcohol (Figure 1).17 This equilibrium has two consequences: First, it increases the solubility of the KF salt due to the increased solvation of the fluoride ion.
Second, the fluoride ion becomes less basic due to hydrogen bonding, and the product of the SN2 reaction is more favorable than E2, enhancing the selectivity (Figure 1).51,52 Based on this effect, a large diversity of hydrogen bond donor species can be used, resulting in different performances.
evidence.section_context: Introduction: proposed preferential-solvation mechanism

evidence.claim: A universal nucleophilicity scale cannot be constructed, but kinetically useful rankings can be made when reaction partners are restricted to carbon electrophiles.
evidence.quotation:
Keywords: kinetics; electrophilicity; nucleophilicity; linear free energy relationships; organocatalysis; intrinsic barriers The answer to the title question is plain: A general nucleophilicity scale cannot exist!
It is well-known that carbocations and protons show selectivities towards alkenes, arenes and amines, which differ considerably from those of metal cations or halogens X 2.I n this lecture it will be shown, however, that useful rankings of nucleophiles can be made on the basis of kinetic experiments, when only carbon electrophiles are considered as reaction partners.

evidence.claim: A single reference electrophile provides only a limited kinetic comparison window; unreactive combinations and diffusion-controlled reactions cannot be ranked by their bond-forming rate constants.
evidence.quotation:
Nonactivated arenes and alkenes on the very left of Fig.
3 do not react at all, while carbanions and enamines on the very right react with the same rates: The rate constants for the very fast reactions are not determined by the rate of the bond-forming step, but by the rates with which the molecules diffuse through the solution.
The consequence is obvious: A single electrophile allows one to compare only a rather limited group of compounds, which differ by less than 14 orders of magnitude in reactivity.
Whichever electrophile will be selected as reference, most nucleophiles will always be outside of this window.[1] For that reason, we have decided to select not one, but more than 30 structurally related electrophiles, each of which allows one to compare a different group of nucleophiles.

evidence.claim: The authors attribute nucleophile selectivity primarily to desolvation, proposing that smaller, more strongly solvated ions react more slowly.
evidence.quotation:
As we accumulate results from the competition experiments, we observe I- > NCS- > Br- ≥ N3 - ~ NC- > Cl- >> AcO- to be the reactivity scale towards the diradical 4.
This is not an intrinsic reactivity scale of these nucleophiles.
It reflects only their ease of desolvation, with the smaller, more highly solvated ions being slower (Figure 2.3.1).

evidence.claim: Heating cyclodeca-1,5-diyn-3-ene with tetrabutylammonium salts in CD3CN at 55 °C for 10 hours produced incorporation products from iodide, bromide, cyanide, azide, and thiocyanate; products were identified by 1H NMR and GC-MS.
evidence.quotation:
We performed nucleophilic additions with enediyne 3 a n d tetrabutylammonium (Bu4N+) salts including iodide (I-), bromide (Br-), cyanide (NC-), azide (N3 -), thiocyanate (NCS-), nitrate (NO3 -), and nitrite (NO2 -) in CD3CN at 55 oC for 10 hours.
These preliminary reactions were carried out in order to identify and confirm Nu - addition products b y 1H NMR and GC -MS.
As observed before in our group,[8] halides (excluding F-) react with the para-benzyne to afford 1-halotetrahydronaphtalenes (6).
Moreover, other anionic nucleophiles react with the diradical intermediate; incorporation of NC-, N3 -, and NCS- was also observed.
GC–MS analysis showed volatiles with m/z corresponding to M+ = C10H10(Nu)D (mass spectra can be found in the Appendix C).

evidence.claim: The trimethylborane-basicity scale failed to explain the inactivity of R-pipecolic acid despite its high calculated basicity, indicating that an initial-attack steric probe does not capture all later mechanistic reactivity, including enamine nucleophilicity.
evidence.quotation:
The 6-membered R-pipecolic acid (13), however, has been reported as inactive in the aldol reaction [37] but exhibits the highest TMB and proton basicity of all the cyclic amino acids investigated.
Hence, its inability to catalyze the aldol reaction does not seem to be due to more pronounced steric constraints in the initial nucleophilic attack but will be situated in a different step of the catalytic mechanism.
Indeed, previous studies have shown that enamines derived from nucleophilic addition to a piperidine ring have a substantially lower nucleophilicity than enamines derived from nucleophilic addition to a pyrrolidine ring [51, 52].
This difference in reactivity is explained by a larger pyramidalization angle of nitrogen in the 6-membered piperidine-derived enamine, resulting in a reduced p-character of nitrogen, and a reduction in the conjugation between the nitrogen lone pair and the double bond of the enamine [52, 53].
evidence.section_context: Results and discussion: limitations of using amine trimethylborane basicity to predict the complete catalytic cycle.

evidence.claim: 文中转述Williams提出的机制：gramine对炔属促进剂进行aza-Michael加成形成两性离子A，继而C–N键解离产生azafulvene B，并由亲核试剂捕获；本文作者另行提出，促进剂被竞争性Michael加成淬灭以及azafulvene被其他亲核物捕获可能造成副反应。
evidence.quotation:
Later, Williams reinvestigated the efficacy of simple alkynyl esters, e.g. ethyl propiolate1b, as the promoter of the deaminative coupling of gramines with active methylenes, particularly malonate deriva- tives.17 The C−N bond activation was proposed to occur through aza-Michael addition on the acetylenic ester generating the zwitterionic intermediateA.
Then, C−N bond dissociation with departure of an enamine fragment would deliver the reactive 3-methylene-3H-indole (or azafulvene,B), ready to get trapped by the in situ generated enolate.
First, complications might arise from the competitive Michael addition of the corresponding nucleophile to the acetylenic reagent20,21 to afford side product III (reagent quenching, vide infra), a process that would be increasingly likely (larger k5) as the electrophilicity of the acetylenic reagent increases.
Complications might also arise from the competitive trapping of (protonated) azafulvene intermedium B by any adventitious nucleophilic species (Nu′), e.g. another molecule of gramine, to end up in formation of side-products II′, and particularly gramine-derived dimeric species.8a,22 Guided by these mechanistic considerations, we decided to test the ability of various electron-deficient acetylenes to promote the deaminative coupling between gramine 3a and iminoester 8a as the model reaction (Table 1).

evidence.claim: In DRM, carbon deposition can deactivate metal catalysts by covering active sites, blocking reactant access, obstructing pores, impairing diffusion, and eventually causing mechanical damage or bed blockage.

evidence.section_context: Deactivation of metal catalysts: carbon deposition

evidence.claim: The author proposes that TBHP decomposes on the Au-Pd surface to form radical species that abstract hydrogen from toluene and lead to benzyl alcohol; benzyl alcohol is then proposed to oxidize to benzaldehyde, followed by further oxidation to benzoic acid.

Chapter 4-Solvent free oxidation of toluene 104 4.4.3 General proposal on plausible mechanistic pathways on toluene oxidation using Au-Pd based on supported nanoparticles catalyst and TBHP as an oxidant Based on the experimental data, the following plausible reaction path ways can be proposed (Scheme 4.
1): (i) TBHP can decompose on the metal surface to produce surface tBuO• and OH radicals. tBuO can abstract H from toluene forming tert-butanol (which was detected experimentally) whilst the resulting toluene derived alkyl radical can react with OH to form benzyl alcohol ; (ii) TBHP can decompose to tBu  and OOH radicals at the surface of the gold -palladium particles and the OOH radicals can abstract H from toluene forming hydrogen peroxide with t he resulting toluene derived alkyl radical reacting with surface OH to form benzyl alcohol.
Other reaction pathway was the oxidation of benzyl alcohol leads in the first instance to the formation of benzaldehdye.
Further oxidation of this molecule leads to the production of benzoic acid, as shown in scheme 4.3.
However, other side reactions are also possible.

Following treatment with TBHP, the EPR spectrum changes markedly (Figure 4.10b); the majority of the Pd + signal disappears, the bulk Ti 3+ remains visible and a new signal assigned to the superoxide radicals (O2 -) is observed; the measured g values of g1 = 2.003, g2 = 2.004 and g3 = 2.024 and line width are consistent with a non-vacancy Ti4+...O2 - coordinated site for a ‘side-on’ ionically bonded conformation. [25] This species is considered to be derived directly (from TBHP decomposition) or indirectly (by reduced Ti 3+ centres reacting with molecular oxygen) fr om TBHP, as it is not present when THBP is absent; e.g. direct
Chapter 4-Solvent free oxidation of toluene 110 exposure of the Au -Pd/TiO2 catalyst to oxygen does not generate this signal in the absence of TBHP.
There was no evidence of a hydroperoxy (HO 2 ) species or other oxygen centered radical (peroxy) which have been previously identified on P25.[26] When the sample was subsequen tly treated with TBHP/toluene (f igure 4.10c), the superoxide signal disappeared completely and a new inhomogeneously broadened symmetric signal with g = 2.004 was formed.

This is clearly evidenced by the fact that when it recovered and dried the catalysts after TBHP addition (f igure 4 .10b) the O 2 - signal remained.

Identification and Location of Atomically Dispersed M-Nx-Cy Active Site The sluggish ORR is dependent on the specific active sites in the catalyst; however, the configuration of the active site in case of pyrolyzed M-N-C catalysts remains unclear. [56] From theoretical and experimental results, several types of active sites are proposed (Figure 1).

However, some alternate coordination structures for active sites have also been suggested, including; M-N 4/C species, M-N 2/C- edge, macrocyclic M-N 4/C species, and graphitic nitrogen N-C species.
Nonetheless, the current data could not provide suffi- cient evidence for the overall picture.[57] Additionally, Jia et al.[58] designed 3 types of active sites containing Fe-N 4/C moieties (Figure 2) and proposed that during ORR in acidic media there were different switching behaviors of Fe-N4 and were associated with a dynamic structure of Fe III/FeII redox transition.
